item.title: Flock CEO Defends Surveillance Tech Amid National Backlash
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from TechCrunch: Flock's founder and CEO Garrett Langley doesn't think the risks of introducing surveillance technology at scale outweigh the rewards. "If we want to live in a society where, if you commit a crime, you have a higher probability of being held accountable, we shouldn't pause progress," Langley said, speaking onstage during a panel at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 in San Francisco on Wednesday.
During the interview, the controversial founder of the surveillance maker of license plate cameras and other recording devices deflected hard questions about the criticism Flock now faces -- which has since led to canceled contracts and even layoffs. Instead, Langley tended to respond to questions with anecdotes from conversations with police chiefs and city leaders across the United States, and tales of the supposed numerous crimes Flock has solved, rather than offer tangible solutions to people's concerns.
In doing so, Langley positioned Flock as an advance in technology that was somewhat inevitable. He stressed that if people wanted to live in a better society -- that is, one with reduced crime -- they would have to offer up their privacy in return. [...] "Technology, at its core, in its definition, is just doing things better. It's not doing things perfect," he said. "Driverless cars, I think, is a fair analogy. Driverless cars, I think, are definitively safer than human drivers. And when there's one accident, I don't think the answer is to shut down driverless cars. The answer is to say, 'Hey, let's talk about how we prevent more accidents in the future.'"
[...] From Langley's answers, it's clear that the ethics around how Flock should be used is a decision he would much rather leave up to others. "We don't want to tell city leaders how to do their job," he noted. "We will provide recommendations, we'll provide defaults, but we're going to minimize the number of mandated features, functions, and policies," he said. Langley went on to argue that society too often judges technology "not on how it compares to the past, but how it compares to perfect." He acknowledged that "Flock is far from perfect" but maintained that its technology helps police departments compensate for staffing shortages and improve public safety.
When pressed about potential abuse and privacy concerns, Langley offered few specifics, instead arguing that safeguards could be implemented without disrupting police operations. He insisted the benefits of what Flock offers outweigh the controversy. "There's millions and millions of people who have a better life today because [of] Flock," he said, adding that "it's worth it because one day they might be a victim."

item.title: Cops Play Hide And Seek About Using Spy Tech To Avoid Scrutiny And Bad PR
item.author: Karen Gullo and Adam Schwartz
item.content:encoded: Some authorities are responding to these concerns by trying to hide what they’re doing. Police departments are telling officers not to mention ALPRs when stopping vehicles and concealing their use of ALPRs to avoid citizens’ public records requests. Concealing the use of unpopular spying tools isn’t anything particularly new for law enforcement—cops have been doing it for years—but it’s just as wrong now as it was 20 years ago.These practices prevent the public from knowing about and questioning how agencies are spending taxpayer dollars on spying technologies and holding them accountable. This is especially troubling when many towns are signing contracts with Flock and other ALPR vendors with little to no public oversight. The practice also violates disclosure obligations, allows cops and prosecutors to hide their tactics from judges, and cheats defendants from being able to challenge the use of evidence gathered by spy tech from being used against them.404 Media recently revealed that in its usage policy for Flock ALPR cameras, one county in Iowa tells police to keep them a secret when detaining people: “DO NOT MENTION ALPR USAGE TO THE OCCUPANTS OF THE VEHICLE,” the policy document reads. “DO NOT MENTION ALPR USAGE IN YOUR REPORT OR COMPLAINT UNLESS ABSOLUTELY NECESSARY.” If writing a report about an incident, police are told to say they used “county resources” in making a stop instead of acknowledging use of ALPRs.In Houston, police officers are likewise instructed to “be as vague as permissible” about why they are using Flock because the searches they run on Flock’s surveillance system could be obtained via public records requests.There is growing public alarm about the threat to civil liberties posed by ALPR cameras and reports of police abusing the tech by using it to spy on their exes. Some cities have the cameras covered up, and others are cancelling their use of ALPR networks. Two states have recently stepped back from ALPRs. This trend is certainly not lost on law enforcement agencies. Hiding the fact that they’re using ALPRs from Flock and other vendors is one way of avoiding scrutiny and bad PR.But law enforcement and their spy tech vendors keeping people in the dark about the surveillance technologies trained on them predates the Flock backlash by decades. For example, AT&T built a powerful phone surveillance tool for police, called Hemisphere, in the mid 2000s, and the company required agencies not to use evidence gathered by Hemisphere in court unless there was no other admissible evidence. If evidence obtained through Hemisphere was used, police were required to recreate it through a traditional subpoena, a process they called “parallel construction.” We called it “evidence laundering.”Likewise, police and prosecutors have taken far-reaching steps to hide from the public and courts their use of cell site simulators, also known as stingrays. Police have used these devices, which trick cell phones into connecting to them instead of phone towers to try locating suspects, to obtain people’s location data without a warrant by deceptively obtaining basic pen register orders from courts. Pen register orders are for obtaining call log data and police don’t need to prove they have probable cause to get one.In Baltimore, for example, a judge concluded that law enforcement had used a standard pen register order to intentionally hide its use of a Stingray from the court in violation of its legal disclosure obligations, leading to a landmark 2015 privacy ruling that cops need a warrant to use the device.That didn’t stop police from continuing to try to pull the wool over the eyes of courts and defense attorneys when they used stingrays, however. Prosecutors have accepted plea deals to hide their use of cell-site simulators and have even dropped cases rather than reveal information about their use of the technology. U.S. Marshalls have driven files hundreds of miles to thwart public records requests.Fortunately, our commitment to shining a light on the use of surveillance tech is just as strong, if not stronger, than law enforcement’s quest to hide it. We’re working with privacy advocates and community groups to bring awareness about existing and emerging spy tools that threaten civil liberties and we’re encouraging policymakers and lawmakers to do more to restrain warrantless mass surveillance and stop it before it ever takes hold. If you’re curious about whether your local police have contracts for ALPRS or other surveillance technologies, you can search EFF’s Atlas of Surveillance.

item.title: Targeted ads delivered 0-click exploits to install mercenary malware
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: Researchers say that mercenary hackers laced ads with zero-click exploits that installed sophisticated malware on the devices of targeted individuals when they did nothing other than load a website or open an installed app.The finding, published Thursday by the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab, said the incident is likely to be the first confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered through targeted ads. The attacks, which worked on iOS and Android devices, are particularly pernicious because they work without requiring any interaction from the target and are invisible unless users run special forensic hardware or software. Citizen Lab said it confirmed that AdFection, as it named the campaign, infected 45 devices at international media organization Al Jazeera in 2024 and 2025.“This investigation should… serve as a clear warning signal to news organizations around the world that they may be being actively targeted via this new threat,” Citizen Lab researchers wrote. “This targeting may happen both in newsrooms and to individual journalists, editors, and other staff members.” Their report went on to say: “The distribution of spyware via targeted ads represents a security risk not only for potential victims but also for states and civil society at large.”

item.title: First-Ever Public Confirmation of 'Zero-Click' Spyware Delivered Via Targeted Ads
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Citizen Lab says it has documented the first publicly confirmed case of zero-click mercenary spyware being delivered through targeted online ads, a technique it calls "AdFection." "There has been a lot of buzz that online ads can be used to identify and automatically hack targets with pinpoint precision, but now for the first time, we have concrete technical evidence showing this process in action," said Bill Marczak, a researcher at Citizen Lab. The Guardian reports: Citizen Lab, a digital investigations research unit at the University of Toronto, said it believed dozens of devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera had been compromised by spyware delivered through ads run by Discover-Tech, which describes itself as a specialised digital advertising agency. According to Citizen Lab, Discover-Tech operates a software platform called Controlium that allows its clients to "mass-profile and deanonymize" internet users then covertly hack targets with third-party spyware. Unlike infections that rely on people interacting with links or files, the spyware requires no interaction from the victim to be installed, making it a new delivery technique, Citizen Lab says. The infections happen without a user's knowledge, and in a matter of seconds, according to Citizen Lab.
"[The online advertising] ecosystem is being weaponized at a massive scale to profile millions of users, then silently infect targets with zero-click mercenary spyware," the report says. According to the report, Controlium is able to harvest a user's identity and IP address when the user is shown a seemingly benign custom-created ad -- for example, for a digital game or a telecoms service. If the user has been selected as a target for hacking, a mercenary spyware firm can then send a malicious code containing spyware to their device, the researchers say. They say that millions of users worldwide have been served ads by Discover-Tech since 2024, including in Yemen, Brazil, Mexico and Czechia. [...] The full extent of the targeting allegedly enabled by Discover-Tech is unknown. Citizen Lab's findings join mounting evidence that the opaque arrangements underpinning the world of online advertising can be leveraged for surveillance.

item.title: Meta and Apple Bring Muse Spark Open AI Model to Mac Studio
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Meta has released Muse Spark Open, an 816-billion-parameter open-weight model optimized to run locally across two 512GB M5 Ultra Mac Studios using Apple's MLX framework. Meta says it's the "most capable U.S. open-weight model to date." MacRumors reports: Muse Spark Open has 816 billion total parameters with 42 billion active parameters and a 1 million-token context window. It is meant for coding and agentic work, and Meta says it excels at extended tasks, multi-step reasoning, and software engineering. The new Muse model was tuned to run on Mac Studio, and Meta says the Mac Studio paired with Muse Spark Open is the "best way to run a powerful model on your own desktop."
From Meta: "Apple's unified memory architecture lets the M5 Ultra's integrated GPU use up to 512 GB per Mac Studio, so two machines can hold an entire model. And the chip's 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth is fast enough to read the small slice each token needs. The result is two Mac Studios behave like one supercomputer with a terabyte of unified memory." Apple hasn't released the 512GB Mac Studio as of yet, but it's supposed to be coming later this month. It won't be cheap, because the 256GB Mac Studio is already priced over $10,000.

item.title: Trump-Appointed Judge Calls Out ICE For Lying
item.author: Tim Cushing
item.content:encoded: This is now as common as breathing. ICE does stuff. Arrested people invoke their rights. ICE shows up in court. The court expresses its anger at ICE’s tactics and lies. Thousands of habeas cases filed by migrants have ended with the courts siding with the arrested migrants. It’s actually more than at this point, but the only thing the administration counts is the arrests. The addition of poorly trained ICE officers to a blend of federal agencies all focused on making chief advisor/ghoul Stephen Miller’s racist fantasies a reality has resulted in the routine violation of rights, as well as the actual murders of American citizens.So far, we’ve mostly heard angry words from federal judges all over the nation. That may change eventually since the government clearly can’t be deterred by being told it’s in the wrong pretty much all the fucking time. There are only words here too, unfortunately. Hopefully, the anger expressed here will be converted into meaningful sanctions against ICE and the DOJ, but until then we will have to satisfy ourselves with knowing all of this is now part of the public record. Trump did manage to stack the most important court in the land — something that has paid off more often than not during his second term as president. If there’s a silver lining here, it’s that most of his court appointees are more interested in serving the law, rather than serving a guy who thinks he was elected king.And so it goes here in New York — one of Trump’s favorite targets due to its resistance to his malignant strain of MAGA. The streets have been swarmed by federal officers almost constantly since early last year. That has resulted in the expected jump in arrests and detainments. Not pictured: any respect for long-respected due process rights or even the barest minimum of Fourth Amendment adherence.A federal judge in New York reprimanded the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency on Monday, accusing its officers of lying, lacking proper training and fabricating records to cover up illegal arrests.Judge Brown wrote that immigration agents involved in the arrests had given “inconsistent, false and misleading testimony” in court, and said that they had probably perjured themselves. He found that the officers were inexperienced, possessed little understanding of the law and used “false testimony to conceal these failings.”What’s detailed in the order [PDF] issued by Trump appointee Gary Brown is the sort of corrupt cop shit we always hoped would mostly be relegated to James Ellroy novels and David Simon series. But what’s been exposed by Trump’s anti-migrant animosity is an agency that firmly believes it can arrest whoever it wants and fix it in post — something greatly encouraged by the Supreme Court’s “Kavanaugh stop” non-ruling. This only deals with one of several plaintiffs making similar arguments about ICE’s arrests. But its telling nonetheless.Agents allegedly arrested petitioner based on a physical description and photograph of one target. Yet the description disproves the match: the target was five inches shorter and 80 pounds lighter than the petitioner. As to the photograph, the team leader acknowledged upon cross-examination that “it’s very easy to see they’re two different people.” Trying to legitimize petitioner’s arrest, ICE issued a post-hoc sworn administrative warrant containing false information and later issued a Notice to Appear. At the hearing, the officers proffered inconsistent, false and misleading testimony.The result is troubling: compelling evidence here belies the ICE agents’ reflexive invocation of misidentification as an excuse for erroneous arrests. Particularly problematic in this case, the evidence suggests that ICE attempted to support their unsupported misidentification argument through false or misleading documentation and testimony. The claims of misidentification here prove baseless, the arrests were procedurally deficient and legally invalid, and ICE agents falsified official records trying to conceal their illegal actions, which included significant injury to a U.S. citizen.Two things should be noted, remembered, and retained as ammunition to use against this administration. First, ICE agents just arrested a guy and then worked backwards to justify the arrest, even though the person they arrested didn’t resemble anything in the narrative ICE hastily erected post-arrest. Second, this whole chain of injustices was inflicted on an actual — you know, the exact people Trump believes are inherently better than anyone else.Here’s the rough equivalence a thousand words disputing ICE’s lies and deflection as officers, supervisors, and government lawyers attempted to salvage something from this illegal arrest that was illegal when it involved a purported migrant, but is at least doubly so when it ended with ICE officers tossing a US citizen in jail. Here’s ICE (and the court notes that some of the officers had almost zero experience [thanks Trump!]) pretending a 5’7″, 110-lb. person is indistinguishable from the purported “target” of the puportedly “targeted” arrest — someone who weighed in at 180 lbs. (at least!) and stood six feet tall. ICE tried to lie its way out of this. But surveillance video provided by a local business showed ICE officers (with weapons drawn) ambushing Concepcion as he peacefully walked to a barber shop. Conception never saw the officers until they threw him to the ground violently, which immediately disproves the claim that the target of the arrest was trying to avoid apprehension. It also disproves nearly everything ICE Team Leader John Katepodis stated in court and on his paperwork as he helped his officers work backwards from an unjustified arrest. First, he states that he “incorrectly testified” regarding what database information was accessible onsite and states that the EARM system “was available to me and my team on our cellphones during the surveillance,” which included the “height, weight and build” of the two targets. Thus, contrary to the testimony he offered at the hearing, Katepodis now claims that the information about “height, weight and build” was available to his team during the operation. Katepodis further attempts to alter his sworn testimony that he was unaware of whether his supervisor had issued the warrant at the time of the arrest, by now stating that “it was [his] understanding that an I-200 warrant of arrest was issued” prior to the arrest. Again, this contradicts his testimony at the hearing, during which Katepodis testified that his supervisor told him “he was going to issue the I 200,” acknowledged that he “didn’t have the warrant yet” and had been “told that an I 200 was going to be issued.” Finally, Katepodis tries to explain his apparent falsification of the warrant by certifying it was served by him in the Bronx, when service was made by someone else in Manhattan. Katepodis suggests that it “was my understanding that the certificate of service for the I-200 required the location of the arrest and where Petitioner was locatedat the time the I-200 was issued.” This is largely irrelevant, as it is clear from the testimony that Katepodis had no idea when or whether the administrative arrest warrant was issued.The ICE Team Leader calls this “incorrect” testimony. Most normal people — including some judges — call this “perjury.” It’s clear from the record that no arrest warrant supporting the arrest of Concepcion existed (and how could it?) before ICE officers arrested him. The document claiming to support this arrest was created ICE had already arrested the wrong person.[T]he Court notes that subsequent to petitioner’s detention, ICE agents prepared a substantially false administrative warrant in an attempt to rationalize their actions. The warrant purports to establish “probable cause to believe that [Almonte] is removable from the United States . . . based upon biometric confirmation of the subject’s identity and a records check of federal databases that affirmatively indicate . . . that the subject . . . lacks immigration status.” DE 7-1. The claim that database queries checks could “positively identify” petitioner appears spurious as, without any immigration record, petitioner would not appear in any ICE database from which he could be positively identified.Unfortunately, there are no sanctions to be had here. Yet. The court is giving ICE one more chance to explain itself before it moves forward with sanctions or any further investigation of its own. I would assume sanctions of some sort will be the end result here, because every time ICE has been given a chance to explain its actions, it just ends up digging a bigger hole. If this does actually result in ICE officers and DOJ lawyers being bench-slapped, I would absolutely expect Trump to start mouthing off about “activist” judges, even though the one he’s complaining about is one he hand-picked for the job. If nothing else, this should prove Trump isn’t quite the wheeler-dealer he makes himself out to be. He’s a terrible judge of character (so to speak). And you know what they say about that: if you can’t immediately spot the sucker in the room, the sucker.

item.title: Nidal Hasan’s Public Execution Is Off, But Propagandists Are Still Using Him as a Martyr
item.author: Matthew Gault
item.content:encoded: Last week, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth announced the Pentagon would the execution of convicted killer Nidal Hasan. Today, Trump said the execution would move forward but that it . But the propaganda damage is already done. Experts who watch terrorist spaces online told 404 Media that Hasan is already turning up in memes, videos, and recruitment material for groups like Al Qaeda.Hasan—a former US Army Major who had once attempted to contact Al Qaeda—killed 13 people and injured 32 others at Fort Hood in 2009. He was shot and captured at the scene and later sentenced to death. Hegseth’s plan to livestream Hasan’s execution and the furor around it brought Hasan and his crimes back into the spotlight 17 years later. Hasan has mostly been a forgotten figure in Islamist and extremist circles, but is now once again a fixture of their propaganda.“It's already started,” Moustafa Ayad, research chair in global Islamism and counter-terrorism at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue, told 404 Media. “We're already seeing edited videos in support of Nidal Hasan, and they're specifically based around how he's a martyr and that his legacy lives on.”In one image Ayad shared with 404 Media, Al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP) referred to Hasan as a “heroic mujahid brother” then quoted Osama Bin Laden. “The day America makes this decision, it will have made a decision to execute whoever among you falls captive.” According to Ayad, an Al Qaeda affiliated propaganda group made Hasan the feature of its newsletter last Friday. “So it's being viewed in that sense already in these ecosystems as he is a hero, and it's going to be used for recruitment and potentially galvanizing inspiration,” Ayad said. “We're talking about a guy who hasn't really been referenced since 2017 really or that much at all. So it has reignited conversations around his attack, how quote unquote glorious it was, and is being used as a means to to recruit people in some shape or form, and will continue to do so.Ayad also described "rampage" edits of Hasan that are floating around extremists circles online that show footage of Hasan dancing over a number that represents how many people he killed. “You have fed the wolves,” he said. “They now have a thing they can latch on to.” In one TikTok edit viewed by 404 Media, a picture of Hasan with laser eyes throbbed to the beat of electronic music.He added that he thinks the memes and videos are being made by younger people. “I don't think an established guy who remembers the Nadal Hassan attack is going to then go: ‘You know what makes sense? Putting out a dancing Nidal Hasan over his kill count.’ I don't think some 35-year-old dude is doing that,” he said. “You have a younger generation that is now attuned to what he did.”Livestreaming the public execution would have given propagandists more to work with. Online nihilists, gore groups, and Islamists often use footage of death and violence to lure in young people. “Dead ideologues are continually being revered, lionized in ecosystems in support of groups like Al Qaeda, the Islamic State, or any terrorist group,” Ayad said. “If you look at the saint ecosystems around accelerationism, it's a similar thing in which these individuals are the vanguard of jihad.”Mass shooters and ideological killers that receive widespread media attention become online. They enter a cannon of sainted killers, totems that inspire others to commit the same acts. Some researchers have suggested news agencies should report a shooter’s crimes but refrain from naming and showing them, thus depriving them of notoriety and stemming the social contagion.Hasan killed people almost twenty years ago and he was destined to fall out of memory until Hegseth attempted to make a spectacle of his death. “We’re already seeing it being incorporated into talking points, we’re past that,” Ayad said.“He is still going to be labeled a martyr," Ayad added. “Will it be a public spectacle? Not anymore [...] but terror groups and their supporters took advantage of the news to highlight just how much of a contribution Nidal Hasan made to their respective movements.”

item.title: Microsoft Says Windows 11 Is Now 'More Responsive', Runs Better On 8GB of RAM
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft says recent Windows 11 updates have made the operating system up to 20% more responsive by improving memory management and reducing background resource use. "A big part of that work is making smarter use of memory and system resources," says Navjot Virk, corporate vice president of Windows experiences at Microsoft. "We've improved memory management and efficiency across Windows to help keep more of your PC's resources focused on what you're actively doing." The Verge reports: The improvements to memory management now make a "meaningful difference" on PCs with just 8GB of RAM. "Windows can now keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory instead of moving it to slower storage," says Virk. "For example, on PCs with 8GB of memory or less, Widgets load only when you open them, making more than 200 MB of memory available for your apps and other work."
Microsoft has also made Windows Update less disruptive, cleaned up the Widgets section, and finally allowed the taskbar to be repositioned to the sides or top of a display. Windows Hello sign-in has also been sped up, and Bluetooth pairing is more reliable, "including an AirPods pairing experience that's up to 15 seconds faster."
The next big step is a new Windows Search experience that's a lot faster and more capable. [...] It's currently available for Windows Insiders, and Microsoft says it will "roll out more broadly later this year."

item.title: Amazon Launches New Bee 'Personal AI' Devices That Listen to Conversations
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Amazon has unveiled two new Bee "personal AI" devices designed to continuously record, transcribe, and analyze conversations: the $75 wearable Bee Frontier and the $100 phone-mounted Bee Eclipse. Amazon says the devices can generate conversation summaries, surface recurring themes, and recommend actions or purchases, while claiming audio itself is never stored and users can delete transcripts and summaries. CNBC reports: The Bee Frontier is an upgraded version of Amazon's existing wearable that can either be worn on a wrist or clipped to clothing. Similar to earlier generations, the Bee Frontier has up to seven days of battery life, but it's also more expensive, costing $75 compared with its $50 predecessor.
Amazon acquired Bee, a San Francisco startup known for its always-listening bracelet, in July 2025 for an undisclosed amount. Bee bracelets are equipped with artificial intelligence and microphones that can record, transcribe and analyze conversations. The dual mics on the Bee Frontier have upgraded noise filtering, "so it can take note of what matters and ignore what doesn't, even in noisy environments like a crowded restaurant or open office," Amazon said in a blog post.
Amazon also debuted the $100 Bee Eclipse, which functions like other Bee devices, but instead of being worn, the credit card-sized gadget magnetically snaps on to the back of a smartphone. The Bee Frontier is available Thursday, while the Bee Eclipse "will be available soon," the company said.

item.title: Accenture Tells Employees They Can Now Spend Only $29 on Claude Per Month
item.author: Joseph Cox
item.content:encoded: Consulting giant Accenture has told many employees that the company will now only spend $29 a month per person on Claude. Employees subject to the cap, some of whom had been spending as much as $1,000 monthly, are scrambling to find ways to make sure they can keep spending as much as they already are.The news is a snapshot of what continues to play out across all sorts of industries: companies have spent heavily on AI tools, and are now discovering that many users are burning or “chewing” through AI tokens at a rapid clip. In response, many companies have curbed their employees’ AI use. There is a special irony to Accenture doing much of the same, when it is a company that has encouraged its clients to invest heavily into AI.

item.title: Video Game Reverse Engineering Community Shuts Down Because AI Has Made It Too Easy
item.author: Jason Koebler
item.content:encoded: A website that was dedicated to the human endeavor of reverse engineering, “decompiling,” and modifying video games because people using AI to clone and decompile games have fully overrun the community and are far outpacing what human software engineers alone can do. The news comes as AI-coded “clones” of popular enterprise software like the Adobe creative suite and Microsoft Office have gone viral and are seemingly popping up every day, and as people in video game modding communities warn that 'AI decomps' are everywhere. The website decomp.dev said Thursday that it is shutting down because “the community aspect of decompilation has been broken” by AI, and that projects that once required intense collaboration between people with different skills can now be done trivially with AI. The administrator of the website said that it has become impossible to keep track of which projects are primarily human-led and which ones are done by AI.“Historically, matching decompilation has been a brutally difficult, time consuming task, on the scale of years for any moderately-sized game with a number of active contributors,” the pseudonymous admin of decomp.dev, who goes by Encounter, wrote on the site. But recent frontier AI models like GPT-6-Astra have made it trivially easy to decompile a game: “They are significantly better at following complex directions, cross-referencing resources for symbols or debug information, and writing natural code with enough guidance,” Encounter wrote. “It is now clear that, with the right guidance, human input, and code reviews, AI can expedite the decompilation process in a significant way. What is also now clear is that the community aspect of decompilation has been broken.”

item.title: Eleventh Circuit Says Cliffhangers Are ‘Features,’ Not Speech, As It Greenlights Florida’s Social Media Age Gate
item.author: Mike Masnick
item.content:encoded: Apparently we’re in an era where the courts just decide to ignore precedents they don’t like. And that leads us to ridiculous results like yesterday’s ruling in the Eleventh Circuit allowing Florida’s HB3 social media age verification law to move forward. But to understand how messed up it is, you need to know the history of a few different Supreme Court cases, and how the Supreme Court has started undermining earlier precedents, effectively granting power to the Eleventh Circuit to make up its own rules.As a quick primer, these are the historical cases you need to understand, to recognize what a clusterfuck this new ruling is.Reno v. ACLU: Effectively establishes that the First Amendment applies to the internet.Ashcroft v. ACLU: Age-gating online speech to shield kids violates the First Amendment when it burdens adults’ access to protected speech and less restrictive alternatives (like filters) exist.Brown v. EMA: State restricting sales of video games to kids violates the First Amendment.Packingham v. North Carolina: State laws can’t ban people from the internet, even if they commit heinous crimes, as the internet involves too much important speech and services.Then we have some more recent cases that make all this shit trickier:Moody v. NetChoice: Makes clear that internet content moderation is protected editorial decision making under the First Amendment comes up with a weird rationale to make it nearly impossible to challenge First Amendment-violating internet laws until after they’ve done real harm to companies, by saying it’s nearly impossible to pursue a “facial” challenge (basically saying the law as written is obviously fully unconstitutional) as opposed to an “as applied” challenge, specifically challenging how the law is enforced.TikTok v. Garland: Basically saying that despite the cases above, the government can completely ban a website by just stating “national security” and the Supreme Court will ignore all the First Amendment issues.FSC v. Paxton: Says the Supreme Court will ignore the Ashcroft ruling above, as long as it involves naked people on the internet. Then you can demand age verification and restrict kids because naked people are icky.So, that brings us to this new ruling in the Eleventh Circuit regarding HB3, which was Florida’s attempt to broadly age verify internet services. The key parts require social media platforms that have “addictive features” (as defined by Florida) to block anyone under the age of 14 from creating an account, and then requires parental consent for 14- and 15-year-olds. In short, it requires age verifying everyone and blocking many users from these services.The trade groups CCIA & NetChoice challenged the law, and the case went through many twists and turns, including a district court judge pointing out that adults freaking out over whatever new thing kids are into is a moral panic that happens all the time, and we shouldn’t immediately assume that just because politicians are screaming about “protecting the children” that we need to believe them. At one point a judge refused to grant an injunction because (the judge said), the trade association that filed the case (CCIA) couldn’t show that any of its members faced imminent harm.Soon after that Florida sought to enforce the law against Snap, a member of CCIA. Eventually, the district court issued a preliminary injunction on the law, though the Eleventh Circuit then put a stay on the injunction, with a dissent from Judge Robin Rosenbaum, who makes a ton of important points. As I said, lots of twists and turns.However, now the Eleventh Circuit has come out with its latest ruling reversing the district court’s preliminary injunction (and vacating it as to the facial challenge), and it’s a fucking mess. Notably, it’s a totally different panel — Judges Newsom, Luck, and Tjoflat — than the earlier ruling, and so this new ruling doesn’t even have the kind of thoughtful dissent Rosenbaum issued last time through this court, and the ruling is worse off for it.First, the similarities to Brown v. EMA should be obvious, but the panel here says that this law is more like the TikTok case, and thus the ruling in Brown doesn’t really apply:HB3 more closely resembles the law at issue in TikTok than the one in Brown. HB3 is facially content neutral: It regulates social-media platforms based on their functional capabilities and features, not the content they communicate. The law neither references the substance of the speech on any platform nor draws distinctions based on it. Put differently, HB3 applies to platforms wholly without regard to the topics discussed or the ideas or messages conveyed on them. Truth Social is just as likely as Instagram to be affected by HB3 so long as (1) a proportion of minors under 16 spend an average of at least two hours a day on it; (2) it uses infinite scrolling, push notifications, auto-play, or livestreaming, or displays user-engagement metrics; and (3) it selects content algorithmically for users. Fla. Stat. § 501.1736(1)(e). And tellingly, neither a platform nor a user can “avoid or mitigate” the effects of HB3 by “altering” the substance of any posted expression. TikTok, 604 U.S. at 71 (quoting Turner I, 512 U.S. at 644).HB3’s justification is also content neutral: to “protect[] children from [social-media] addiction and associated mental-health harms.” Br. of Appellant at 36. That purpose is “unrelated to the content of expression” on any given platform, and it doesn’t “reflect[] disagreement with the message such speech conveys.” TikTok, 604 U.S. at 72.To put it simply: that is garbage. The reason for Florida’s law is not content neutral at all. It is passing these laws because it doesn’t believe kids should have access to all sorts of constitutionally protected speech. That is important. The claim that it is to “protect children” could equally apply to all sorts of speech, such as books, TV shows, movies, or video games (remember what the Brown case is about?), but we (and the courts) immediately recognize that has clear speech implications, and you can’t wave them off as “content neutral.”On top of that, the claim that this is just about “capabilities and features” not content ignores that many of those features (as established in cases like Moody) are, in fact, the expressive (First Amendment-protected) speech of the platforms themselves, which the state is effectively banning. To call the law content neutral, even as it calls out specific editorial features, just seems fundamentally incorrect.Even more incredibly, the Eleventh Circuit literally seems to suggest that states can regulate all sorts of speech that might make people more interested in content as “features” rather than speech. CCIA had pointed out that the law is not at all content neutral because it puts rules on internet speech that doesn’t apply to speech in other mediums, and uses “cliffhangers” in books as an example.In particular, CCIA emphasizes that HB3 prohibits addictive features only on websites, not on other “services that disseminate speech”—like, for instance, “books that end in cliffhangers.”The Eleventh Circuit dismisses this in a footnote… suggesting that cliffhangers and other tricks to get people to read more in books because they’re “features” not “speech.”Further, the analogy to literary devices that make books more engaging—like cliffhangers, shorter chapters, or serialization—simply reinforces Florida’s contention that it’s not focused on speech and the accompanying ideas, topics, and messages, but rather on features that in and of themselves are agnostic as to content.I am… flummoxed by this. Cliffhangers are features, not speech? Have any of these judges ever read a book? Short chapters are features not speech? What? Under the logic of this ruling, a state could issue a ban on short chapters and cliffhangers as being too “addictive” and the Eleventh Circuit says that would pass intermediate scrutiny and be just fine.And that alone should tell you how preposterous this ruling is.CCIA pointed out how much protected speech gets stifled under this law, but the judges dismissed it. They claim (incredibly) that the law doesn’t “burden” too much speech:HB3 doesn’t “burden substantially more speech than necessary” because it (1) calibrates its restrictions by age, (2) regulates minors’ creation of social-media accounts, not necessarily their access to the platforms themselves, (3) covers only those platforms that have been determined to induce heavy use by children, and (4) applies only to platforms that use both algorithms and one of several addictive features.But that’s simply wrong. It absolutely burdens a ton of protected speech for users under the age of 14. The “calibrates its restrictions by age” ignores that it requires a full block on those under 14, even though there may be plenty of age appropriate speech online for those under 14 (my under 14-year-old middle schooler regularly watches educational videos on YouTube, for example).Also, it simply ignores that anonymity is protected under the First Amendment, and this law effectively ends anonymous accounts for everyone, since age verification has to cover all users. How did the court address that? It didn’t. Search the ruling for “anonymous” and you get:At least with the last time through this court in the Rosenbaum dissent, she was able to highlight the issue of anonymous speech. Here, the court just ignores it. Poof. Doesn’t matter.The court also says all this is fine because it doesn’t restrict access, only account creation:Second, even among those to whom HB3 does apply, the law restricts only their ability to create their own accounts, not their ability to access social-media platforms per se. The creation of a social-media account is a commercial act—a business transaction. Even a minor—indeed, even a young child—may continue to use the platforms provided he either (1) uses his parents’ (or someone else’s) account or (2) gains access without an account.But there are plenty of platforms that restrict access to only those with an account. And, again, it also restricts how platforms decide what features to offer, which is its own burden.Separately, the court claims that this law is fine because it only targets platforms to which kids are “already addicted.”Third, HB3 targets only the platforms to which many minors are already addicted. As a reminder, a platform comes within HB3’s purview only if at least 10% of daily active users under 16 years old spend an average of two hours or more per day on it. Fla. Stat. § 501.1736(1)(e). Together with its other limitations, HB3’s tailoring efforts fall within the broad range of potential legislative solutions that intermediate scrutiny permits.Even leaving aside the fact that repeated research suggests claims of social media “addiction” are way overblown, it’s also wrong about the law. Just because people use something an average of two hours or more a day does not, definitionally, mean “addicted.” People spend hours a day reading, playing sports, or watching TV, but we don’t claim those are addictions that need to be regulated. The data here (from the Bureau of Labor Statistics) is a bit outdated, but it found that people tend to watch more than two hours of TV a day. Do we claim that everyone is addicted to TV?Also, nothing about the law is focused just on those who use the platform that much. It bans those who use it for just minutes a day as well if they’re 13-years-old. Arguing that it’s narrowly targeted makes no sense at all.Bizarrely, the panel then claims that because the platforms can change what features they offer kids, that shows that this doesn’t burden speech. Really.And fourth, HB3 operates not as an outright prohibition of platform usage but rather as a “conditional ban” of sorts—namely, on platforms’ use of addictive features and algorithms. See TikTok, 604 U.S. at 74, 77. The law applies only to platforms that use a combination of algorithms and addictive features and that succeed in keeping many minors on them for an average of at least two hours a day. See Fla. Stat. § 501.1736(1)(e). Refraining from using either algorithms or addictive features, or remaining below the temporal threshold, exempts a platform from the law’s application.Right. So, you just admitted that it impacts the editorial decision making of the platforms, the very thing the Supreme Court said in Moody that is protected by the First Amendment.And while the Packingham case makes it pretty clear that you can’t ban people from websites because there is so much important speech there, again the panel here dismisses that because it’s just banning “a subset of minors” rather than “all sex offenders” as was the case in Packingham.Unlike HB3, which applies only to a subset of minors, the statute there covered all registered sex offenders. And unlike HB3, which applies only to a subset of social-media platforms, the law there defined the covered sites exceedingly broadly; it included “commonplace social media websites like Facebook and Twitter,” as well as “websites as varied as.” Id. at 101, 106 (majority opinion). And unlike HB3, which restricts account creation but doesn’t limit access to the platforms per se, the statute there forbade any usage of the covered sites. Id. at 101. HB3 is tailored in a way that the law at issue in Packingham was not.I literally do not understand what they mean when they say HB3 is different because it only applies to a “subset of minors.” It applies to minors under 14 with a ban on account creation, and also applies to 14- and 15-year-olds by requiring parental approval for account creation. That’s… way more people than “all sex offenders” (unless Florida has more registered sex offenders than children under 16, which seems like a different kind of problem).Then we get to the FSC v. Paxton issue. When the Supreme Court ruled in that case last year, we highlighted that the reasoning of the ruling was quite clearly limited to non-First Amendment protected speech, which they claimed included content that would be obscene to minors. But (importantly) we were sure it would open up the floodgates to people claiming it applied much more broadly to all sorts of internet services.And… that’s exactly what is happening here, and the Eleventh Circuit judges seem to think it’s no big deal to magically expand the FSC ruling to mean you can age restrict First Amendment-protected content too.CCIA contends that, by contrast, HB3 prohibits certain minors from accessing protected speech. That may be so, but Free Speech Coalition didn’t purport to establish a constitutional outer limit; nothing in the Court’s reasoning there precludes a state from imposing an age-verification requirement that operates to limit minors’ access to some protected speech—provided, of course, that it does so in a content-neutral manner.That’s literally wrong. The majority decision in FSC quite clearly says it is okay to restrict it the content is “obscene” to children, and thus not protected. Straight from Clarence Thomas’s decision:Because H. B. 1181 simply requires proof of age to access content that is obscene to minors, it does not directly regulate the protected speech of adults…. On its face, the statute regulates only speech that is obscene to minors. That speech is unprotected to the extent the State seeks only to verify age. And, the statute can easily “be justified without reference to the [protected] content of the regulated speech,” because its apparent purpose is simply to prevent minors, who have no First Amendment right to access speech that is obscene to them, from doing so.So, I’m honestly baffled that the Eleventh Circuit now claims that SCOTUS’s ruling wasn’t limited to only unprotected speech. It was core to Thomas’ ruling.The Eleventh Circuit then takes other parts of the FSC ruling out of context, to say that because it mentioned age verification in other contexts (offline) being okay, that means they can extend it to protected speech:To the contrary, everything the Court said in Free Speech Coalition seems to point in the other direction. The Court emphasized, for instance, that “[r]equiring age verification is common when a law draws lines based on age.” Id. at 479. It noted that many states require proof of age to buy alcohol and tobacco, as well as to obtain licenses to carry a handgun, to drive, and to marry.Buying alcohol, tobacco, or firearms is, notably, not speech. Neither is driving or marrying. What the fuck are the judges even doing here?Finally (though, not surprisingly, due to the awkwardness of the Moody ruling), the court rejects CCIA’s “facial” challenge, saying that because some of the platforms covered by this law might host speech that is unprotected under the First Amendment, CCIA hasn’t shown that the law’s unconstitutional applications substantially outweigh its constitutional ones. Incredibly, just pages after insisting that FSC v. Paxton isn’t limited to unprotected speech, the court turns around and leans on FSC’s unprotected-for-minors category to argue that some covered platforms host unprotected speech.Put differently, just because users are “engag[ing] in speech” on a platform doesn’t mean that their expression is fully protected by the First Amendment. Id. There are all kinds of social-media platforms featuring—or even if not featuring, permitting—all kinds of expression. To be sure, much of that expression is fully protected. But some isn’t. The Supreme Court has held, for instance, that certain kinds of speech enjoy no First Amendment protection at all—e.g., incitement, true threats. See Brandenburg v. Ohio, 395 U.S. 444 (1969) (incitement); Counterman v. Colorado, 600 U.S. 66 (2023) (true threats). Other kinds of speech enjoy constitutional protection when exhibited to adults but not when exhibited to children—pornography being the most obvious example. See Free Speech Coal., 606 U.S. at 496.It may well be true that most expression on most social-media platforms is indeed protected. But not all of it is, at least not with respect to all users. So, for instance, imagine a platform that hosts only unprotected speech—say, Incitement.com or TrueThreats.com. A law restricting children’s (or anyone’s) access to it wouldn’t implicate the First Amendment at all and would trigger only rational-basis review. A law restricting access to a site that hosts speech that is protected for adults but not children—like pornography—would implicate the First Amendment, but a contentneutral restriction—like an age-verification requirement—would be subject only to intermediate scrutiny. See Free Speech Coal., 606 U.S. at 495. Accordingly, even if HB3 “imposes the same onerous restriction” on every platform, Dist. Ct. Order, June 3, 2025, at 43, that restriction could well be subject to different levels of scrutiny, potentially leading to different outcomes.My response to that is a giant eye roll and “come on.” And, even the judges on the Eleventh Circuit realize “come on, you can’t be serious” is the only logical response here, but insist that the Supreme Court’s ruling in Moody requires such an outcome:One might interpose a “come on” objection at this point: Surely, the argument would go, the overwhelming majority of platforms to which HB3 applies overwhelmingly host protected speech. And if, as CCIA insists, the law’s application to those websites would be unconstitutional, then the law’s unconstitutional applications would probably substantially outweigh the constitutional ones. But however intuitive, that sort of impressionistic judgment won’t satisfy Moody’s stringent demands. Whether or not it’s likely that the collective content of the platforms within HB3’s ambit is overwhelmingly protected, CCIA bears the “burden” of demonstrating both (1) the universe of the law’s applications and (2) that the invalid applications substantially outweigh the valid ones.And, perhaps the ruling in Moody is to blame for this part of it, but when an appeals court has to admit how nonsensical this reasoning is, it seems like a sign that the Supreme Court should reconsider its silly requirements for facial challenges in Moody.There is a concurrence from Judge Kevin Newsom, who points out that the Supreme Court is effectively all over the map regarding this “as applied” vs. “facial” challenge stuff post-Moody, noting that other recent SCOTUS rulings suggest “as applied” challenges for intermediate scrutiny may not really be allowed either, and then coming around to the obvious conclusion that this might mean that under recent SCOTUS doctrine, the state can pass all sorts of speech suppressing laws with no way for the courts to block them. And, uh, yeah, dude, that’s why these rulings are so damn concerning.But if the Supreme Court’s point in Moody was to make as-applied challenges the new normal in First Amendment litigation, it seems strange that the same Court—the same nine people—would have then turned around less than two years later and nixed as-applied challenges for the whole range of First Amendment claims that call for intermediate scrutiny. And I don’t think it makes me a result-oriented hack to worry that a combination of Moody’s new (or newly emphasized) limitations on facial First Amendment challenges and a prohibition on as-applied challenges in a host of contexts would lead to, well, a lot less protection for traditionally safeguarded speech.In the end, I’ll confess that I’m not quite sure what to make of B.P.J.’s statement casting doubt on the viability of as-applied challenges to laws that trigger less than strict scrutiny. But before exporting it to the First Amendment context, I think it’s wise to await a clearer signal from the Supreme Court.While he doesn’t come out quite that far to say it, by suggesting it doesn’t make him a “result-oriented hack,” he is kinda pointing a finger at “the same nine people” on the Supreme Court who have made these conflicting decisions that make it effectively impossible to stop speech suppressing laws, even with the First Amendment. And they result-oriented hacks, as some of us have been pointing out (though, realistically, he’s just talking about the “conservative” six who were in the majority of the BPJ case, which effectively puts the kibosh on as applied challenges for anything that qualifies for less than strict scrutiny.Either way, this ruling makes a mess of free speech online in really damaging ways. Admittedly, some of that is due to the “results oriented hacks” at the Supreme Court, but the Eleventh Circuit’s interpretation of the rulings in Brown, Moody, Packingham, FSC, and a variety of other cases, suggests a do over is absolutely necessary. Hopefully this ruling gets tossed under an en banc hearing or, somehow, by the “results-oriented hacks” at the Supreme Court. With other circuits also having trouble remembering the First Amendment exists online, one hopes that the Supreme Court steps in and reminds them.

item.title: Uber Begins Self-Driving Robotaxi Trial In Manchester

An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Guardian: Uber has begun a trial of autonomous vehicles on the streets of Manchester as it looks to bring robotaxis to cities around the UK. The first self-driving cars are operating, using the technology of its partner firms Pony and Verne, with whom Uber recently launched Europe's first autonomous taxi service in the Croatian capital, Zagreb. Uber said it was "excited to take this first step toward making this technology accessible to people across the UK."
In social media posts, Verne said it had "started our autonomous vehicle testing in Manchester," while Pony said there were "plans to bring robotaxis to the city" and that testing was under way. The tests involve the company mapping the streets of the city in north-west England with a safety driver behind the wheel and no passengers. Limited passenger services started last month in London, but with a safety driver in the front seat of cars supplied by Wayve under Transport for London's licensing rules for private hire vehicles.
The next steps are unclear. Opposition from Uber drivers, their unions and the capital's politicians to the rollout of robotaxis is mounting. The GMB and ADCU unions have both said thousands of drivers jobs will be lost and have called for help for those affected. A critical report from London assembly's transport committee this week called for the government to devolve authority over autonomous taxi services. It said there was "considerable uncertainty about many of the claimed benefits of autonomous passenger vehicles", and fears over the impact on public transport and congestion, as well as safeguarding and accessibility for disabled passengers. There has been no official application to launch passenger services in Manchester so far.

item.title: Data Centers Are War Targets Now
item.author: Matthew Gault
item.content:encoded: In 2006, British economist Clive Humby “data is the new oil,” and big tech adopted the metaphor. Twenty years later, a dark side of the truism has been revealed. If the places where oil is refined are valuable targets in a war then so, too, are the places where data is refined. We’ve seen this not just in the Russia-Ukraine war, but also with Iran hitting Amazon Web Services data centers in Dubai in retaliation for America’s strikes on the country. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed strikes on Russian data centers and oil refineries and called them a “symmetrical response" to Russian aggression. Here we have oil and data together again, not as a metaphor in an economics lecture, but in the pronouncement of a world leader defending his country. conducting a war.Three of Ukraine’s strikes hit data centers that belonged to Yandex, Russia’s Google-equivalent, and damaged the company’s supercomputers that housed some of its AI models. The latest attack hit a data center operated by Sberbank, Russia’s largest bank. It’s too early to tell what the effects of the strike on the Sberbank data center will be, but the three strikes on Yandex have disrupted internet and communications across Russia.An online rumor said that the strikes on Yandex had the effect of taking down Russian bot farms, . The effects of the strikes on the civilian population were much more severe. Yandex is ubiquitous in Russia — it has its own app store, payment services, dating services, taxi and bus apps, and email services. The company operates six data centers in Russia and the strikes knocked two of them offline completely. People in Russia have lost access to their email, some of their data is seemingly gone, and taxi and bus apps only work intermittently.ChrisO_wiki, an anonymous researcher who translates Russian social media posts for the western web, chronicled how the Yandex outages are hitting everyday Russians. “A taxi driver from Yekaterinburg says that after the service disruptions, he can no longer view his order history, and the status of trips is updated with a delay,” ChrisO_wiki said in a post on X and Bluesky. “The loss of Yandex's cloud services is also having severe impacts on Russian commercial logistics. Those who work with electronic document management are unable to register incoming goods, severely affecting manufacturers and distributors,” they .Klaudia Klonowska, a who studies the effects of emerging technologies on international law, told 404 Media that attacks on data centers are so new that international law around them is still developing. “You have very limited situations in which they would actually qualify as lawful targets when they're used by the military, and even then, it's very difficult for the attackers to know whether that's happening or not,” Klonowska said.If the data centers are purely processing military data, then they could be legitimate targets, according to Klonowska. But many, if not most, data centers are dual-use, meaning they house both civilian and military data. In many cases, disrupting daily life seems to be part of the point.When Russia struck data centers in Ukraine in September, state-backed news agencies claimed it that supported Ukrainian intelligence efforts and was a lawful target. Ukraine denied the allegation. “So you see how difficult, because of the nature of these centers, it's really to pinpoint what is happening with them and who is using them and for what means,” Klonowska said. “Sometimes [Ukraine] mentions that these data centers contribute to Moscow's revenues that then fuel the war machine. But that's not enough to make them lawful targets. Retaliation is not enough under law.”Klonowska noted that it is civilians who suffer most, not the military, when data centers go offline. “There are questions about proportionality given how widespread the attacks are,” she said. “A lack of internet access for very prolonged periods affects everything. It's all of the civilian services that are being disrupted, which you can imagine also includes things like hospitals, traffic, judicial services, etc. etc.” It’s worth noting that Russia has repeatedly attacked civilian targets in Ukraine, including apartment buildings, public transportation, .According to Klonowska, international and humanitarian law needs to catch up with the issue and that scholars like herself are only just starting to understand the ramifications. “I think there's also another bigger question behind all of this,” she said. “Why have we gotten to the point where we have permitted militaries of various states to use civilian commercial data centers for their military purposes? By potentially using them and relying on them, they have opened them up to the possibility of becoming military targets.”Disentangling civilian and military data probably won’t take data centers off the target list, but it will make international law more clear on which buildings are legitimate targets. It may also change how data centers processing military data are built. “France has recently announced that they have unveiled their underground data center on the outskirts of Paris that will be exclusively for military use,” Klonowska said. “Just as we expect them not to use schools or hospitals or other civilian residential areas to host weapons or other military equipment, we would, I think, increasingly need to mention this in the case of data centers.”The idea that a data center might be a military target is not lost on the American communities facing construction of them in their backyards. America’s nuclear weapons scientists at Los Alamos National Laboratories (LANL) have partnered with the University of Michigan in an attempt to in Ypsilanti Township, Michigan. The people and government of the Township aren’t thrilled about it for a number of reasons and the city attorney has said that the data center would be a “high value target” in wars of the future. Los Alamos pushed back on this in a in September, around the same time Russia was striking data centers in Ukraine. LANL accused the township attorney of creating “that terminology without basis. It should not be interpreted as evidence of a known, specific, or imminent threat to the facility or the surrounding community,” the letter said. “Like other major research facilities, the center would employ appropriate security measures, including controlled access, cameras, and on-site security personnel,” it said. “Los Alamos and U-M would coordinate with local, state, and federal partners on matters related to safety and security.”It’s easy to see where the people of Ypsilanti Township are coming from. When Ukraine struck three Yandex data centers in Russia over the weekend, its drones slipped past Russia’s air defenses. The idea that a town next to a data center, especially one with ties to America’s nuclear weapons programs, could sustain damage if the data center was ever attacked isn’t unfounded. The data centers smoldering in the world’s war zones proved that the township’s fears aren’t theoretical.

item.title: Starlink’s Entry Into Wireless Is Being Wildly Overhyped
item.author: Karl Bode
item.content:encoded: One of the ways Musk fraudulently goosed SpaceX stock value during the IPO was by pretending that the company would very quickly (in just a year or two) grow from just 12 million global Starlink subscribers (just 4 million in the States) to something more akin to 300-500 million. Starlink wants to plunk down thousands of meshed femtocells installed on customer rooftops alongside existing LEO satellite dishes, something one telecom analyst recently stated was “one of the top three dumbest ideas in my four decades of being in this industry.” In part because the femtocells will eat up already dwindling capacity on the increasingly congested network (recall that Starlink customers in some areas already face “congestion fees” as high as $1500). Musk Corp is also leveraging its cozy relationship with the Trump administration to hoover up as much spectrum as they can get their hands on. You might recall that Trump FCC boss Brendan Carr launched an “investigation” into Echostar to specifically help offload their spectrum to Musk. SpaceX also recently bought 14 megahertz of spectrum in the 800 MHz band from investment firm Grain Management, which bought the spectrum from T-Mobile earlier in 2026.The recent purchase was enough to send AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile stocks tumbling:“Verizon closed down 8.75% on the news, its worst day since July 2002. Shares of T-Mobile dropped 13.27% while AT&T fell 9.81%, each notching their own worst days since 2013 and 2000, respectively.”In contrast, the white supremacist’s space company’s stock only jumped around 1 percent for the day. The problem for Musk is multifold. As Dish Network found when it failed utterly to disrupt the sector, it takes a lot more than spectrum hoarding and some greased palms to become a major player in wireless. Actually building a useful network the public wants to use that covers rural and urban markets alike is a massive cash sink investors despise in part because networks take years to finish.The highway of telecom history is positively filled with the gravestones of companies that tried to cleverly out-maneuver giant incumbent telecoms, which are directly tethered to the heart of the Republican party (remember Starry?). Space X and its boosters believe that simply having access to Starlink’s network of Low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellites is some kind of magic wand toward competing in wireless (they’re already partnering with T-Mobile for phone calls in out-of-the-way locations). But even normally staid telecom analysts have been shitting all over Musk’s femtocell plan, pointing out it’s not going to scale well:“Given the laws-of-physics limitations, a Starlink network of small cells would probably have more holes in it than a hiker’s socks. Neither Lum nor Rhodes sees much likelihood of coverage in urban areas that enjoy mainstream and lower-cost alternatives. “It works best in rural because you’ve got fewer choices for fiber and so most customers are there. Where are your customers to repeat it in the city?” said Rhodes. “Well, they don’t exist because they’re not that stupid.”There’s also the fact that Musk companies don’t really believe in customer service, and fail in most every instance where they’ve been forced to try. Both Starlink and Tesla Solar are routinely inundated with stories where customers can’t even get the companies to respond to phone calls or emails. Starlink also consistently isn’t particularly affordable for the folks most in need of access. Starlink is (and will probably always be) a good niche broadband solution best suited for people out of reach of better, faster, more affordable options if they can afford it (rural homes, boats, RVs, wars, disasters). But Musk and Republicans have broadly tried to claim that the technology is some sort of magic bullet for connectivity. To the point where they redirected what ultimately will likely be billions of infrastructure bill taxpayer dollars away from faster fiber networks to Starlink. The actual threat to giants like AT&T and Verizon is limited, though outlets like CBS buried that fact deep in their bullish reporting. Even a best case scenario requires a massive outlay of capital and a half a decade to even get close to begin trying to compete in the space, something SpaceX’s more reality-based investors definitely aren’t going to enjoy.

item.title: Mini Organs Launching to Space For Study On Aging
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Researchers from Mount Sinai, NASA, and Space Tango have launched miniature human hearts and brains to the International Space Station to study how microgravity and radiation affect organs and potentially accelerate aging. "If people are going to be living and working in space, then we need to understand what's going to happen to them," David Sachs, assistant professor of surgery at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, told ABC News. "But also, because it's interesting as a model of accelerated aging for studying people on Earth." From the report: The mini organs launched aboard commercial resupply mission CRS-35 on Tuesday morning from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. They are expected to arrive at the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday. The miniature organs offer researchers a unique opportunity to simulate aging in a much shorter period of time to understand disease and develop treatments. "Six months in space ... is equivalent to about 10 to 20 years of aging on Earth," Kevin Costa, associate professor of surgery at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, told ABC News.
Sachs and Costa are sending up to 16 miniature hearts to the ISS to test how they respond to electrical signals and monitor how they may react to near-zero gravity. The technology, which is integrated into a miniature laboratory called CubeLab, was developed by Space Tango and simulates the natural environment in the human body. "[It is] slightly bigger than a shoebox, and it is a fully automated, miniaturized system," Gentry Barnett, chief technology officer at Space Tango, told ABC News.
[...] As part of the new effort, the team is sending miniature brains, called miBrain, to the ISS. Around the size of a peppercorn, the miBrains reflect models of healthy and diseased brains. By exposing them to the space environment, scientists can see how mini-brains respond and better understand why living in space accelerates aging. Though the mini organs are not full-sized human organs, the researchers say they are good substitutes, cost-effective and don't take up much of the limited space aboard the space station. They also believe discoveries made in space can translate to uses in everyday medical care.
The microgravity environment uniquely allows researchers to study what happens to humans with a sedentary lifestyle or prolonged bed rest, which isn't easily simulated on Earth, Sachs explained. "[The research is] translating to stuff in space, but it's also translating back to the research we do in the laboratory to help people with Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease," Joel Blanchard, associate professor of stem cell biology and regenerative medicine and neuroscience at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, told ABC News. Lisa Carnell, the director of the biological and physical sciences division at NASA, told ABC News that these experiments serve as a starting point for future research beyond low Earth orbit, including to the moon and beyond.

item.title: Schools Across US Protest FCC Plan That Could Disconnect Kids From Internet

item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Schools and libraries from around the U.S. pleaded with the Federal Communications Commission to drop the idea of ending E-Rate, a $2 billion-a-year program that connects students and library visitors to the Internet. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr has criticized school districts for having "experimented with a massive increase in screen time for students," and said E-Rate expanded too far beyond its original purpose of "supporting basic Internet access to schools and libraries for educational purposes." In June, Carr led a 2-1 vote to issue a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) seeking public comment on whether E-Rate should be "limited or sunset to reflect today's extensive connectivity rates."
Carr's proposal could result in E-Rate cutting the discounts that schools and libraries receive for telecom services and equipment, and imposing more restrictions on how E-Rate money can be used. The FCC seeking comment on whether to sunset the program also raises the possibility that Carr might choose to axe E-Rate entirely. The National Association of Elementary School Principals told the FCC that it "strongly supports the continued operation of the E-Rate program and urges the Commission to reject proposals that would eliminate, substantially restrict, or impose new conditions on this essential source of connectivity assistance for schools and libraries." The Carr FCC already scaled E-Rate back last year by ending funding for schools and libraries to lend out Wi-Fi hotspots and for Wi-Fi service on school buses. "Importantly, the FCC does not have the authority to terminate the E-Rate program. The E-Rate program is mandated by Congress, and the FCC is responsible for administering it," the American Library Associated told the FCC.
The American Library Association said "the FCC lacks the authority and expertise to regulate screen time or determine educational outcomes." In a filing, the group pointed out that under U.S. law, determinations about what content is inappropriate for children "shall be made by the school board, local educational agency, library, or other authority responsible for making the determination."

item.title: Epic Games Somehow Gets Even Worse On AI Than Tim Sweeney’s Anti-Disclosure Take
item.author: Timothy Geigner
item.content:encoded: There have certainly been some bad takes on both sides of the AI in video games argument. In one corner, we have the never-AI-ers who reflexively claim that any use of any type of AI in any game is a total disqualifier. No quarter is given to nuance. No daylight is offered for discussion. It might as well be religion to those folks. Then, on the other side, you have people like Epic Games’ Tim Sweeney, who has not only directed his company to go all in on the use of generative AI in gaming, but actually had the chutzpah to suggest that his rival Steam’s inclusion of AI-use disclosures on its storefront are “irresponsible.”But Epic has somehow gotten even worse on AI use than that. Rather than suggesting that generative AI is a tool for use in gaming, which can often mean its use is employed on the perimeter of game-creation, Epic has decided to make the use of AI compulsory.According to a new report by Bloomberg, developers on the game were told to implement an “AI-first” production model using Anthropic’s Claude AI models. The team is not to use any more “hand-written code,” and even artists are being pushed to use the technology that has become a punching bag among actual players. The director of the unannounced game reportedly told developers that all art should be “generated with full AI workflows.”“We’re embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do,” Jake Jones, communications director at Epic Games, said in a statement.It’s hard to overstate just how stupid this is. This isn’t handing artists new and interesting paintbrushes to use. It’s taking their paintbrush away entirely and telling the artists to simply tell a machine what to make. . It’s also completely antithetical to how other game makers have employed the use of AI. This is going to turn off both the public, which generally hates the idea of artistic interruption through the use of AI tools, the pool of artists Epic does and could in the future employ. AI models getting better at coding, certainly. But what Epic is clearly doing is anti-artist for the sake of speed-running development after cutting human employment.The upcoming shooter, which Bloomberg reports was supposed to release in March 2027, has now been delayed due to slow progress and understaffed teams. Despite a $1.5 billion investment by Disney in 2024 for collaborations that include this project, the Fortnite maker laid off 1,000 people earlier this year amid the battle royale’s struggles and the costs of ongoing antitrust litigation.For the group that is dogmatically opposed to the use of AI in gaming, this is their boogeyman come to life. It’s the starkest example of bad corporate behavior enabled by AI that they could want. And it’s very hard to argue against them when there are bad CEOs and bad companies out here pulling this kind of garbage. I won’t even try. I’ll repeat that I think there is a place for this technology as a tool to enable artists and enable more art. But if the gaming industry is too poisoned at this point to allow for that possibility to be employed responsibly, then so be it.

item.title: We’re Asking the Wisconsin Supreme Court to End Warrantless ALPR Searches
item.author: Andrew Crocker
item.content:encoded: Today, EFF joined the ACLU of Wisconsin in filing a petition to the Wisconsin Supreme Court, asking it to rule that the state’s constitution requires a warrant for retrospective searches of ALPR databases used by law enforcement in four cities: Milwaukee, Racine, Kenosha, and Green Bay. We represent a religious organization, the Wisconsin Council of Churches, as well as an individual pastor in Green Bay.As the petition explains:Right now, Automated License Plate Readers (“ALPRs”) are recording the movements of vast numbers of Wisconsin drivers as they seek medical care, attend 12-step recovery meetings, attend religious services, participate in protests, attend political meetings, and engage in many other private, sensitive activities. Law enforcement entities throughout Wisconsin collect, store, share, and aggregate this ALPR data. Then they search it, retrospectively tracking the movements of individuals and entire communities in ways that would have been prohibitively costly, if not outright impossible, before the advent of ALPR technology.We all deserve to be free of warrantless mass surveillance. We all deserve to live in a country where surveillance vendors cannot help police upend our system of individualized suspicion. Religious organizations and officials like our clients have a heightened interest in protecting their location privacy because of the range of expressive associations their work entails, including facilitating gatherings for religious worship, as well as offering pastoral care, confidential counseling, and community support. Likewise, the people who visit houses of worship have a strong right to privacy against police monitoring of when they pray, seek addiction counseling, or attend a domestic violence survivor meeting.This is our second lawsuit challenging warrantless ALPR searches, following Earlier this month, a federal court in Oklahoma became the first to rule that ALPRs are a “type of indiscriminate mass surveillance” and suppress evidence from a warrantless ALPR search. We hope the Wisconsin Supreme Court will agree.Read the Wisconsin Supreme Court petition
